description:
Plants do make noises too. Perhaps not the proverbial growth of grass, but exploding seed capsules are part of the soundscape in the Santa Monica Mountains this time of the year. I noticed it first when I tried to locate a Wing-tapping Cicada and realized that the Vetches fooled me, https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/48232169.

Bigpod Ceanothus trees are even noisier than Vetches because they carry many more fruits per cubic meter. If you wait and listen close to one, you’ll be bombarded with seeds from the exploding, ripe fruits. 

Wikipedia notes about the fruit of these trees: “The inside of the capsule is divided into 3 valves, each valve holding a seed. The capsule dehisces neatly in three at the central band to release the seeds.” And, “Dehiscence is the splitting, at maturity, along a built-in line of weakness in a plant structure in order to release its contents, and is common among fruits, anthers and sporangia. Sometimes this involves the complete detachment of a part. Structures that open in this way are said to be dehiscent. Structures that do not open in this way are called indehiscent, and rely on other mechanisms such as decay or predation to release the contents.”

Dehiscence doesn’t mean there’s necessarily a hiss. In this case it’s a sharp ticking sound. In the background of the recording are a Common Raven and a Northern Mockingbird.

To celebrate the quieter times, I petitioned @finatic, the creator of https://www.inaturalist.org/projects/audio-observations-from-around-the-world, to include maybe a few plants in his project that is animalia only.

description: There were many very tall Black Oaks (Quercus kelloggii) in the area here (at ~3200' elevation)...together with less abundant and much less towering (i.e. scrub to small tree form) Garry Oaks (Quercus garryana). However, trip companions Joyce Gross & Diane Erwin began to suspect some of the towering oaks we were seeing might be Q. garryana as well, though all the candidates we'd been seeing had their leaves too high to examine closely (and the leaves of the two species can look similar at a distance). Fortuitously, this one had a branch hanging down to ground level, so we could examine the leaves closely...and the lobing-pattern and lack of any bristles at the lobe-tips indicated Q. garryana. The ID was reinforced by the presence of galls characteristic of the "white oak group" (see iNat obs 80586516) rather than "black oak group". The truck in the photo is over 6' high, and a direct ratio of the tree height (in pixels) to truck height yielded a rough estimate of over 80 ft high for the oak. But the truck is further away than the tree, and if it were at the same distance it would appear larger due to perspective. Given that...and after measuring from another photo Joyce took with me standing at the base of the tree, I'd estimate the tree was between 50 to 60 ft high. From its great height, this is clearly the nominate variety of Q. garryana. Sierra National Forest botanist Joanna Clines mentioned to me that the small tree varieties of Q. garryana (i.e. Q. g. var. breweri and Q. g. var. semota) were well known & collected from the central Sierra Nevada, but that it would be interesting if we could also find the very tall nominate variety, which had no vouchered records from Sierra National Forest. There are currently only 3 CalFlora records of the nominate variety Q. g. var. garryana from the Sierra Nevada...and they are from significantly further to the south: in Tulare County at Grouse Mnt and near Sherman Pass Rd; and in Kern County near Breckenridge Rd. And although the range map at the bottom of the Jepson eFlora for Q. g. var. garryana doesn't include the Sierra Nevada...the records map there does show 3 points from much further to the north (2 records from the 1890's in Amador County here and here; and 1 from 1997 in El Dorado County). So this observation helps fill a large gap in the Sierra Nevada range for the nominate variety.

Varied Lupine (Lupinus variicolor) is a native, uncommon, perennial plant that grows 2-5dm tall on grassy slopes of coastal dunes, beaches, bluffs and sandy terraces at elevation < 100ft. Stem and leaves are generally spreading-silver hairy or dense-appressed hairy. Flower petals have NO banner spots and can be white, yellow, rose, or purple, often on 1 plant. The back of the banner is glabrous. The keel is ciliate along the entire upper margin. Peak bloom time: April-July.

Lupines (Lupinus genus) are in the Legumes (Fabaceae) family, a.k.a. Pea Family. Legumes are nitrogen fixers and they help sequester carbon in the soil. "The Pea family has 5-petaled flowers, consisting of a wide upper banner petal, two wing petals, plus two lower petals which are fused to form a boat-shaped keel. Many produce heads or spikes, consisting of multiple individual flowers (examples are lupines and clovers). The seed pod is generally a “legume,” a long, flattish pod, swollen by the seeds, and splitting lengthwise along both the top and bottom. Most lupines have distinct clusters of flowers in spikes, sometimes short, sometimes quite tall. Leaves are typically palmately compound, with leaflets ranging from very narrow to broad. It is useful to note whether the flowers are in whorls around the stem. It can also be critical to look at the keel, to see the pattern of hairs. Some are ciliate on both the top and bottom of the keel; some have hairs only near the claw (base), others only near the tip." https://montereywildflowers.com/fabaceae-lupine-per/

Canyon Live Oak (Quercus chrysolepis) is a native, evergreen tree in the Beech (Fagaceae) family. It is the most widely distributed Oak in California. It grows in canyons and on moist slopes in the Coast Ranges and the Sierra Nevada foothills. In mixed woodland, with mild temperatures and moderate rainfall, it grows into a tall tree with a stout trunk and many large upright branches. Leaves are variable, generally oblong to oblong-ovate with an acute tip. Young leaves may be entire or toothed, dark green above and golden below. Mature leaves are distinctly bluish on the lower surface. The acorns are oblong, ovoid or elliptic. The cup is more distinctive. It is shallow with thick, sometimes tubercled scales, and is covered with golden hairs when young. Peak bloom time: April-May.

OAks in general:

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family.
Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

Coast Whitethorn (Ceanothus incanus) California endemic shrub that grows up to 4m (13 ft) tall in maritime chaparral. Stems are ascending to erect and puberulent. Twigs are rigid, thorn-like or not, pale gray to gray-green. Leaves are alternate, evergreen, widely ovate, adaxially (topside) dull green, glabrous to sparsely puberulent, abaxially (underside) gray-green, strigose, 3-ribbed from base, with entire margins. Stipules are scale-like. Petioles 3--12 mm long. Inflorescence is a panicle-like cluster of tiny white flowers. Peak bloom time: March-April.

Buckbrush (Ceanothus cuneatus), a.k.a Ceanothus oblanceolatus or Wedgeleaf Ceanothus is a native shrub in the Buckthorn (Rhamnaceae) family that grows < 3 m high on slopes in Yellow Pine Forest, Chaparral, and Pinyon-Juniper Woodland plant communities.. Stems are generally ascending to spreading. Branchlets are grayish-brown to brown, rigid or flexible, glabrate, puberulent, or tomentulose, with straight hairs straight. Leaf blades are elliptic, oblanceolate, or obovate, one-veined, and opposite. Leaf tips are acute to +- rounded and margins are entire. Flowers white to lavender or blue. Peak bloom time: February-April. Calflora lists 3 subspecies.

description: Our botanical hiking group was intrigued by the many conspicuously yellowed-but-persistent leaves on this "late deciduous" oak. Perhaps "partially deciduous" would be a better phrase here...as there were also still plenty of green leaves attached — even at this late, nearly mid-winter Feb 1st date. Many other deciduous oaks were present in the local area (e.g. Q. lobata and Q. douglasii)...but they had all completely dropped their leaves by this time. The intermediate evergreen/deciduous behavior here, together with leaf characters (i.e. lobing, somewhat shiny upper surface, paler lower surface, vestiture, etc.) suggested this was a hybrid of a deciduous and an evergreen pair of parent species in the "white oak group" (Quercus sect. Quercus). We were thinking perhaps Q. douglasii and one of the local scrub oaks (i.e. Q. berberidifolia or Q. durata). Later, @joergmlpts referred me to this nearby iNat obs...which appears as if it may actually be the same exact tree we saw. And there's also this similar-looking iNat obs 38209307 from very nearby. Both those observations were placed as Q. douglasii...but the observers indicated they suspected they were hybrids of Q. douglasii crossed with a scrub oak. On researching things in the days after our visit, I found a likely candidate: Quercus x subconvexa. It was described by John Tucker in 1953 as a hybrid of Q. garryana (Oregon Oak) and Q. durata (Leather Oak)...both of which are vouchered from the area (indeed Tucker found individuals of each nearby). The agreement is excellent(!) between this oak and the many details of Tucker's description & extended discussion of Q. x subconvexa. Of particular note, diagnostically, are: 1) the lobing pattern of the leaves...each lobe with a short, sharp mucro at its tip; 2) the vestiture of the leaves (uniformly-densely distributed long-rayed stellate hairs abaxially vs. more isolated & widely-scattered tiny clumps of tightly-tufted short-rayed hairs adaxially); as well as the partial deciduousness and paucity/apparent lack of acorns. And, intriguingly, this site appears to by quite near (and perhaps is! ) the type locality for Q. x subconvexa...which was described as a "north-facing slope, elev. 1300 feet" (compare with topo map link here) and "approximately 5 miles north-northeast of Gilroy". I checked on Google Earth and the spot here fits the bill extremely well. Note also that Tucker's voucher labels on all 29 records at this CCH2 link give equivalent descriptions of the (type) locality...though 3 different sets of coords were assigned to those records by herbaria data entry staff. This ACME Mapper link shows: "A" the coords of this observation; "B" the coords given for 18 of the CCH2 records; "C" the coords for 2 of the records; and "D" the coords for 6 of the records. Again, the type locality is described as a north-facing slope "near the top of a hill" (cf. 3rd paragraph here)...which is in accord with our observation site at "A". Points "B" and "C" are in an open grassy area at 200 (resp. 220) meters to the SSE on a southwest-facing slope, while point "D" is 1450 meters to the SSW and far downslope from the hilltop! Those points are not in accord with the description of the type locality site. The strong fit between critical features of this oak with those discernible in photos accompanying 24 of Tucker's 29 vouchers at the preceding CCH link (see also the SEINet links here and here)...as well as the agreement with a preponderance of the many details in the nicely written paper Tucker(1953)... have me fairly-well convinced of the ID here. As an additional landmark, this observation site is just north of two park benches and an interpretive sign along the Mummy Mountain Trail...as seen in the north-facing 7th photo of the series. The oak here had the appearance of a clonal cluster and was distinctive & unique among all the oaks we saw in the larger surrounding area. And from closely studying Tucker's description of the plant(s) and locale, I believe this is the type locality and this is the cluster of (seemingly clonal) plants he was discussing. ---Comments on Individual Photos of the Series--- 2nd Photo: Thumbnail is 16 mm wide. Together with Photos 8-10 here, one gets a sense of the relatively large size of the leaves here...presumably reflective of parentage from the relatively large-leaved species Q. garryana. 6th Photo: Tree-like habitus of Q. x subconvexa at center of photo (it looks like a 2nd smaller individual may also be present to the right). 8th Photo: Abaxial side is shown in the two duller leaves still attached to the twig (at upper right-center & at lower right ); and also for the detached leaf at lower left...all other leaves here exhibit the shinier adaxial side. 9th Photo: View of adaxial (upper) side, with mm scale. 10th Photo: View of abaxial (lower) side, with mm scale. 11th Photo: Pale abaxial side at left vs. shinier adaxial side at right. 12th & 13th photos show detail of abaxial sides. Though it's difficult to make out in the photos (but much better discerned under a well-lit stereo-view dissecting microscope), the abaxial hairs here are somewhat dense and "stellate". In particular, most these stellate hairs had 5-7 relatively-long & straight rays...each ray centrally-attached to the base of the (compound) hair and radiating outward & slightly upward. The attachment of the rays was visually very subtle to perceive under a stereo-view dissecting scope at 40X magnification and could easily be overlooked. I wasn't able to discern it with a hand lens. And I don't think I was able to capture it well in the last two photos here...though I tried.

“Hairy Armpits” on leaf underside at vein junctions (where 2ndary veins meet primary vein)  distinguishes Coast Live Oak from other Live Oaks (Quercus genus). I wondered, what organism  causes those "hairy armpits" ? My quick, simplified answer when asked will be: "The hairy armpits on the CLO are most likely Mite Dormitories"
Here are some great replies/theories: 

1. "I believe the hairs are trichomes, the purpose of which is thought to be preventing water loss from the stomata, however, some hypothesize that they are 'dolmatia' which harbor mites, the purpose of which is unknown. Maybe the mites are predatory on CLO herbivores, or maybe they're just taking advantage of the habitat." INat yerbasanta.

2. "I think the prevailing hypothesis is that they function as dolmatia - places for arthopods to live - in this case, mites. There's an idea that the mites either eat fungi or prey on herbivorores that would otherwise damage the leaf. A 2020 paper by Coltharp et al. found support for the dolmatium hypothesis, but didn't find support for the predation or fungivory - perhaps because of small sample size and not necessarily because the process doesn't occur. So, mites live there, and there might be a benefit to the tree." INat fredwatson

3. "Yes, the tufts of hair in the vein axils on the lower side of Q. agrifolia leaves are trichomes, one of the most versatile of all plant structures (hairs extending from epidermal cells). In some plants like sage they are biochemical factories storing up all sorts of plant secondary compounds to discourage herbivery, or they can be involved in seed dispersal such as cotton bolls, or catching insects in carnivorous plants. My favorites are trichomes in Atriplex where they are used to accumulate salt, die, and break off, so that the plant can grow in salty soils. In many plants, leaf surfaces with stomata are also covered with trichomes to increase the "boundary layer" of still air and slow evaporation by limiting convection. But I don't think that is what is going on here in the Coast Live Oak or the hairs wouldn't be limited to "armpits." While they have shown that predatory mites do preferentially inhabit the "dorms," they haven't shown that there is any benefit to the oak. So it remains a mystery...
Domatia https://www.jstor.org/stable/27099566" INat hkibak

Pines haven't borne cones for a couple of years. Bedrock is granite, liberally exposed, highly grusified. description:
"One of these things is not like the other" 

I was walking around Summit Park today. Almost all of the native trees here (let alone the oaks) are valley oaks, but up on the hill from the path nearby, I saw one large, slightly bushier oak with seemingly more pastel-colored leaves. I realized after taking a closer look that it appears to be a blue oak. It looks very old based on the trunk size (>a century old). I could not find any acorns on it, but that was also true for the valley oaks nearby for the most part (too many acorn-eating animals nearby)

Almost all of the oaks here (in the woodlands) are blue oaks, Tucker's oaks, and their hybrids (Alvord's oaks). There are also some California scrub oaks in the chaparral regions nearby. 

Honestly, the lobing makes me think that this has Q. lobata in it as well (all of the surrounding oaks are seemingly Q. john-tuckeri, Q. douglasii, hybrids of the former, and Q. berberidifolia, but Q. lobata is found less than a mile away), but the other traits and surrounding environment are all suggestive of Alvord's oak imo.

description: On 10/3/74 [James Griffin vouchered a discovery of *Quercus palmeri*](https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/new_detail?PGM1704&YF=0) in the Clear Creek area of San Benito County. At that time this was a new, isolated, northerly station for this unusual species. Griiffin returned about 3 weeks later with his botanist friend and CA oak maven John Tucker, and together they collected a number of additional vouchers. At that time *Q. palmeri* went by the name *Q. dunni* (after the remarkable late-1800's naturalist & collector George Dunn, see Jepson's brief bio here). Later Griffin & Tucker published a 1976 Madroño note on the newly discovered station. Motivated by the above, and a prior interest in this species, I was eager to look for these Palmer Oaks...and joined Joyce Gross & Alice Abela to search for them, almost 50 years after Griffin & Tucker's voucher collections. After planning and walking a route with a number of promising point locations suggested by the Madroño note & voucher labels, we seemed to have struck-out on our "best candidate sites" and were becoming somewhat discouraged. But crossing a creek after the road we were on faded out, Joyce came upon a smaller trail following the SW side of the creek, and within a few hundred feet there were 3 or 4 clumps of Palmer Oaks growing on the steep bank above the trail :-). Note that zooming-in on the iNat inset map above, the observation icon appears to the NE of the trail shown there...but that's an artifact of errors in either my camera's GPS reading, the rendering of the trail on the map, or both. The rough location is correct, but the trail follows the SW side of the creek there...and the Palmer Oaks are rooted along the eroding upper edge of the tall bank just SW of the trail. Palmer Oak is thought to be a relict species that had a more widespread and continuous distribution in Pleistocene and Pliocene times. Except for a few areas in southern California, northern Baja California, and Arizona (see SEINet map here), nowadays it is usually found in small isolated stands of a few individuals, which are often clonal groupings...and these stands are typically many miles apart (e.g. ten, twenty, or much more!). One particular clonal colony growing high on a granitic summit in the Jurupa Hills of Riverside County, CA has been estimated to be 13,000+ years old in this 2009 paper. The plants here were growing in 3 or 4 "clumps" of scrub to small tree-like stature — each with one to several small, clustered, multiple trunks. They appeared less clonal in growth form than other Palmer Oak groupings I've seen...but may have been clonal. I have no idea how old these plants currently are, but they may have difficulty persisting for a truly long time into the future at this site — as their roots are being undercut by erosion of the bank above the old jeep road/trail and adjacent creek. This may be exacerbated in part by human impacts...recent motorcycle tracks were apparent, and a large branch had been cut off and was lying by the trail (visible in 8th photo above, at center left). Some branches were overhanging the trail...and Palmer Oaks are notoriously rigidly-branched with leaves that are viciously stiff & spine-margined! Wouldn't want to hit a branch, or even of a spray of twigs, while speeding past. In addition to the Jepson eFlora treatment for *Q. palmeri*, more info is available on the SEINet page here.

OAKs (genus Quercus) in general:

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family.
Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

Muller's Oak (Quercus cornelius-mulleri) A.k.a. Desert Scrub Oak. Formerly called Quercus dumosa.
It is a native oak in White Oaks (Section Quercus) and in the Beech (Fagaceae) family that grows up to 3 meters (10 feet) tall, generally in granitic soils, in chaparral and pinyon woodland plant communities. It is a bushy, shrubby, and densely branched with tangled twigs. Leaves are evergreen, leathery and thick, oblong, ovate, or narrowly obovate with margins entire or 4--6-toothed. Leaves are adaxially (upper surface) sparsely puberulent and abaxially (underside) whitish and densely fine-tomentose. Habitat is chaparral and pinyon woodland, generally growing in granitic soils. Muller's oak was segregated from the Quercus dumosa complex in 1981 and was found to warrant species status of its own.

"The 25,500-acre Pioneertown Mountains Preserve descends from the high piney 7,800-foot ridges into the Pioneertown Valley. The small community of Pioneertown is surrounded by conservancy-owned volcanic mesas, the Sawtooth Mountains, and preserve lands leading to the San Bernardino National Forest. The preserve has year-round riparian corridors in Pipes Canyon and Little Morongo Canyon. It is an important landscape linkage between Joshua Tree National Park, San Bernardino National Forest, and the Big Horn Mountains Bureau of Land Management Wilderness.
In 2006, the vast majority of the Joshua trees, pinyon pines and junipers at Pioneertown Mountains Preserve were killed in a 70,000-acre lightning-caused fire of unprecedented magnitude. Today, much of the preserve is going through natural vegetation succession. Some scientists predict that fire succession and climate change will favor scrub oak and Joshua tree plant communities that may replace the pinyon forests. The fire laid bare the region’s rich geological backbone."

Coast Live Oak (Quercus agrifolia) A.k.a. CLO, is a native, long-lived tree (up to 125 - 250 years) in the High-latitude Oaks (Subgenus Quercus) and Beech (Fagaceae) family. Quercus agrifolia is by far the most common Oak tree on the Monterey Peninsula, CA. Leaves are evergreen, oval, cupped or spoon-shaped (adaxially convex). “Hairy armpits” at leaf veins on underside of CLO leaf distinguishes it from other Quercus species. Margins of mature leaves have sharp spines that are very noticeable when you sit in the leaf litter. Acorns (fruits) are long and slender.

Per Jepson eFlora: Coast Live Oak grows "(6)10--25 m, evergreen; top wide; trunk bark furrowed, +- checkered, +- gray. Leaf: 2.5--6(9) cm; petiole 4--15 mm; blade generally widely elliptic to round, generally adaxially convex, +- dull green, abaxially glabrous to densely tomentose, dull, pale green, tip rounded to spine-toothed, margin rolled under or not, weakly spine-toothed. Fruit: cup 10--16 mm wide, 8--15 mm deep, obconic, scales thin, +- not tubercled, +- glabrous, +- brown; nut 25--35 mm, slender, ovoid, distally acute, shell woolly inside; mature in year 1. "

What causes those fuzzy, white "hairy armpits" where primary vein meets 2ndary veins? Answer: Mite Apartments. Per INat fredwatson: "the prevailing hypothesis is that they function as dolmatia - places for arthopods to live - in this case, mites. There's an idea that the mites either eat fungi or prey on herbivores that would otherwise damage the leaf. A 2020 paper by Coltharp et al. found support for the dolmatium hypothesis, but didn't find support for the predation or fungivory - perhaps because of small sample size and not necessarily because the process doesn't occur. So, mites live there, and there might be a benefit to the tree."

Canyon Live Oak (Quercus chrysolepis), a.k.a. Canyon Oak, Golden Cup Oak or Maul Oak is a native, evergreen tree in the Beech (Fagaceae) family that grows in canyons and on slopes in many plant communities, including near the coast and in the desert. It is the most widely distributed Oak in California. Leaves are flat, not cupped, leathery, oblong to oblong- or round-ovate, adaxially (top-side) dark green, abaxially (underside) golden or pale, puberulent when young, and glabrous in age. Leaf tips are acute to abruptly pointed. Margins are variable and can be entire, or spine-toothed. Acorns are oblong, ovoid, or elliptic. The cup is more distinctive. It is shallow with thick, sometimes tubercled scales and is covered with golden hairs when young. Peak bloom time: April-May. Peak flowering time: April-May. Sky Lupine (Lupinus nanus) is a native, annual, common, fragrant plant in the Legumes (Fabaceae) family that grows 1--6 dm (up to 24 inches) tall in grasslands, coastal sage scrub, and in foothill woodlands. Flowers are generally whorled (spiraled) at distal stem. Petals are usually bright blue but can also be lavender, pink, or white. The narrow white banner spot with tiny bluish-purple dots is one of the key, easy-to-see characteristics to identify Sky Lupine. As with other Lupines, the banner spot turns reddish-violet with age. Keel upper margin is ciliated near tip and lower keel margin is glabrous. no tooth on keel, ciliate on upper margin distally, larger overall size, and bluish-purple, spotted white banner rules out Miniature Lupine (Lupinus bicolor). Peak bloom time: March-May. Fruit is a long, hairy pea pod with 4-12 seeds.
In Monterey County, CA, Sky Lupine (Lupinus nanus) can be seen growing in great profusion in meadows, especially along Highway 68 near Toro County Park, adjacent Mark’s Ranch, and in Fort Ord National Monument.

description:
This has to be Q. x morehus, since there are no Q. agrifolia anywhere close to this location.  In contrast, there are abundant Q. kelloggii and Q. chrysolepis in the immediate area.

One key to discriminate Q. x morehus says it "usually" has more than 13 "major secondary veins".

The key was written by Al Keuter, and he kindly clarified for me that a "major secondary vein was one that was connected to the primary vein (midvein) on one end and traveled reasonably directly to its terminus at the edge of the lamina".

I count 11 major secondary veins in the first pix in the sunlit portion of the leaf, plus there are probably 2 in the area covered by the shadow from my finger, for a total of 13 major secondary veins.

description:
A potential refind of this 1947 collection: https://www.cch2.org/portal/collections/individual/index.php?occid=2468116

The plant was growing roadside and weed whacked as a result. It was also growing in very similar conditions to the plant near Valyermo, just above a wash with Joshua Trees, Junipers, and Prunus fasciculata. 

The other oaks in the area were Qcuercus cornelius-muelleri. This Q palmeri differed by having distinct spines on the leaf margin, a twistier warping of the leaves, wider leaves, green rather than grey leaves, and a clonal growth habit that seems more dense than the one for QCM.

This could be the only Q palmeri in the bounds of JTNP.
